prompt.context: Syzygy Supercomputers is a large international fully-integrated computers and communications company with annual revenues of approximately $20 billion U.S. In the past several years, the company has seen a steady decline in profits. The CEO has asked us to look into this problem.
prompt.question: How can Syzygy Supercomputers get back on track?

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape like?
clarifying_info.a: There are several players in the market, but everything has remained stable from a competitive standpoint.

clarifying_info.q: How do Syzygy's cost drivers (COGS, SG&A) compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: COGS, SG&A, and other profitability factors are on-par with Syzygy's competitors, except for R&D, about which you should ask specifically.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any other details about the company?
clarifying_info.a: Only the information already provided is available at this time.

exhibits.title: Syzygy's Historical Costs, Revenues and Profits
exhibits.shows: A time-series chart of Syzygy's revenues, total costs, and profits over several historical years
exhibits.data: Annual revenue (~$20B scale), cost lines, and profit trend showing steady decline in recent years

exhibits.title: Worldwide Telecom Computing Market (Today)
exhibits.shows: A market map showing multiple product segments with bar-like rectangles representing Syzygy and competitors' market shares across five product categories
exhibits.data: Five product categories shown; rectangle heights represent market share of Syzygy and closest competitors in each category; rectangle widths represent category market size

exhibits.title: Syzygy's Absolute vs. Relative Market Share
exhibits.shows: A bubble chart plotting Syzygy's five products on X-axis (Absolute Market Share) and Y-axis (Relative Market Share vs. closest competitor), with bubble size proportional to Syzygy's total revenues in that category
exhibits.data: Five unlabeled bubbles; X-axis = Absolute Market Share (AMS); Y-axis = Relative Market Share (RMS = Syzygy share / closest competitor share), where >1 means Syzygy is market leader; bubble diameter = Syzygy revenue in category

exhibits.title: Companies' R&D vs. Degree of Technical Leadership
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot comparing major competitors' R&D spending (as % of revenue or absolute) against customers' perception of their degree of technical leadership, with a normative band indicated
exhibits.data: Syzygy and named competitors (including Cray Research and Sonic Wave) plotted; a normative band shows expected R&D-to-leadership relationship; Syzygy sits below the normative band

exhibits.title: Syzygy's R&D Expenses and Selling Prices for Supercomputers
exhibits.shows: A breakdown of Syzygy's R&D spending by feature category alongside the corresponding customer willingness-to-pay (selling price uplift) for each feature
exhibits.data: Feature-by-feature comparison of R&D expense vs. customer willingness to pay, showing some features where R&D cost exceeds revenue generated

framework: 1. Examine historical performance: review revenue, cost, and profit trends over time to quantify and confirm the decline
2. Analyze market dynamics and competitive positioning: understand Syzygy's share in each product segment relative to competitors
3. Deep-dive into profitability drivers: examine COGS, SG&A, and — critically for a hi-tech company — R&D spending
4. Identify the root cause: isolate which cost driver or revenue driver is out of line vs. competitors and vs. returns
5. Develop recommendations: address the specific cost/revenue misalignment and consider portfolio rationalization

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 1. What does the historical trend tell you, and what would you investigate next?
questions.guidance: Candidate should confirm profitability has been declining despite relatively stable revenues, implying costs have grown faster than revenues. Should ask to see market position data to understand whether the issue is competitive or internal.

questions.prompt: You are given Exhibits 2 and 3 together. Which product on Exhibit 3 corresponds to which category in Exhibit 2?
questions.guidance: Candidate must correctly map bubbles on Exhibit 3 back to product categories in Exhibit 2 using the relationship between AMS (X-axis = height of Syzygy rectangles in Ex. 2), RMS (Y-axis = ratio of Syzygy rectangle height to competitor rectangle height in Ex. 2), and bubble size (Syzygy revenues = AMS × category size). Correct mapping: Product 1 = Custom Applications, Product 2 = Supercomputers, Product 3 = Telecom Equipment, Product 4 = Satellites, Product 5 = Operating Software.

math.setup: RMS = Syzygy market share / closest competitor market share. If Syzygy is market leader, RMS > 1. Bubble diameter ~ Syzygy revenue = AMS × category size.
steps: Identify which product in Ex. 2 has the tallest Syzygy rectangle (highest AMS) → maps to rightmost bubble on X-axis in Ex. 3
Identify which product has Syzygy's rectangle taller than all competitors (RMS > 1) vs. shorter (RMS < 1) → determines Y-axis position
Match bubble sizes to Syzygy revenue by category
Product #1 (Custom Applications): high RMS, moderate AMS, moderate revenue bubble
Product #2 (Supercomputers): high RMS, high AMS, large revenue bubble
Product #3 (Telecom Equipment): moderate RMS, moderate AMS
Product #5 (Operating Software): low RMS, low AMS, small bubble — Syzygy is not the market leader
math.answer: Product 1 = Custom Applications; Product 2 = Supercomputers; Product 3 = Telecom Equipment; Product 4 = Satellites; Product 5 = Operating Software

questions.prompt: Given Exhibit 4, what is the key insight about Syzygy's R&D spending?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe that Syzygy is the only major competitor whose R&D spending falls below the normative band (the expected relationship between R&D investment and perceived technical leadership). Despite spending slightly more than Cray Research and Sonic Wave, Syzygy enjoys less customer perception of technical leadership — indicating its R&D dollars are being misallocated.

questions.prompt: Given Exhibit 5, what is the specific problem with Syzygy's R&D allocation, and what should be done?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that Syzygy is spending on features that do not generate customer willingness to pay above the R&D cost. The absolute R&D expense on certain features exceeds the incremental revenue those features produce. The candidate should recommend either (a) cutting R&D on features consumers won't pay for, or (b) redirecting the same R&D budget toward features that generate willingness to pay exceeding the investment.

math.setup: For each feature: Net value = Incremental selling price (customer WTP) − R&D expense per unit sold
steps: Identify features where R&D expense > customer WTP uplift → these destroy value
Identify features where customer WTP uplift > R&D expense → these create value
Prioritize or increase investment in value-creating features; cut or redirect value-destroying ones
math.answer: Syzygy should stop investing in features whose R&D cost exceeds customer willingness to pay, and redirect that spending to features where WTP > R&D cost, thereby improving net profitability without reducing technical competitiveness in areas customers value.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond R&D rationalization, what other strategic moves should Syzygy consider given its market position across the five product segments?

categories.name: Portfolio rationalization
ideas: Exit Operating Software (Product 5): small and shrinking share means economies of scale, network economics, and the experience curve all work against Syzygy in this segment — it should divest or discontinue
Double down on market-leading segments (Supercomputers, Custom Applications) where Syzygy already has scale advantages working in its favor

categories.name: Competitive moats in strong segments
ideas: Invest in features that reinforce technical leadership where Syzygy is already the market leader
Use scale advantages in top segments to reduce unit costs and improve margin

categories.name: R&D efficiency
ideas: Implement a voice-of-customer process to validate customer WTP before committing R&D budget to new features
Benchmark R&D ROI against competitors to ensure spending is within the normative band and generating perceived leadership

categories.name: Go-to-market / pricing
ideas: Improve pricing to capture full WTP for features customers value
Bundle high-value features into premium product tiers to improve revenue per unit

recommendation: Rationalize R&D spending by immediately cutting investment in product features where R&D expense exceeds customer willingness to pay, or redirect that budget to features where WTP clearly exceeds cost
Exit the Operating Software segment (Product 5) where Syzygy lacks scale and competitive dynamics (network effects, experience curve) structurally disadvantage it
Concentrate resources on Supercomputers and Custom Applications — segments where Syzygy is the market leader — to deepen competitive advantages and leverage economies of scale
risks: Cutting R&D could damage long-term innovation capacity if not done selectively — must distinguish features customers don't value from foundational R&D
Exiting Operating Software may have integration or contract dependencies that need to be unwound carefully
Competitors may invest in segments Syzygy exits, potentially growing stronger
next_steps: Conduct a detailed feature-by-feature WTP analysis across all product lines to prioritize R&D reallocation
Evaluate divestiture options for the Operating Software business
Set R&D spending targets that place Syzygy within the normative band of technical leadership perception
Establish ongoing R&D ROI measurement tied to customer willingness-to-pay metrics
